extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, scientists, and students of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding precepts for assembling natural history and applying an inductive method to discover axioms from experiment; addresses what to include in observation, how to avoid errors of authority and premature generalization, and the aims of scientific inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the most common objects in natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: “No judgment can be formed of that which is rare or remarkable, and much less anything new brought to light, without a previous regular examination and discovery of the causes of that which is common, and the causes again of those causes” — therefore the most common objects must be admitted into our history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of common phenomena to investigate include gravity, the rotation of the heavenly bodies, heat, cold, light, hardness, softness, rarity, density, liquidity, solidity, animation, inanimation, similitude, difference, organic formation. Anti-pattern: taking these as self-evident and only reasoning about rare occurrences; failure to examine common causes impedes understanding of rare/new phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit mean and even filthy particulars into natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: “Many parts of our history will contain much that is light and common, mean and illiberal, too refined and merely speculative... With regard to the meanness, or even the filthiness of particulars... such subjects are no less worthy of admission into natural history than the most magnificent and costly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not exclude observations because they seem sordid or insignificant; valuable information may emanate from mean instances (analogy: the finest odors sometimes produced from putrid matter such as musk and civet). Anti-pattern: refusing to record or consider 'mean' particulars on aesthetic or status grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer experiments that afford light (knowledge) over immediate profit
rubrics_metrics.description: “We look for experiments that shall afford light rather than profit... the knowledge of simple natures, when sufficiently investigated and defined, resembles light... affords access to the general mysteries of effects.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim experiments to reveal simple natures and principles that illuminate many effects, even if not immediately commercially useful. Analogies: light (enables many things) and elements of letters (separately of no use but essential for speech). Anti-pattern: privileging only experiments with immediate material utility and dismissing those that provide conceptual insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid speculative subtilties and discursive efforts before deriving axioms from experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: “All subtile disputes and discursive efforts of the mind are late and preposterous, when they are introduced subsequently to the discovery of axioms... They otherwise catch and grasp at nature, but never seize or detain her.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experiment to establish axioms first; only then are subtle disputes appropriate when weighing experiment and deriving axioms. Anti-pattern: scholastic habit of elaborate disputation and reasoning from abstract principles without experimental grounding; wasting effort on words or common notions instead of things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject reliance on authority and ancient opinion in place of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “We reject every kind of fiction and imposture; and think it of no more consequence to our subject, whether future discoveries were known to the ancients... than it would be... to know whether the new world be the island of Atlantis.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust the evidence of facts rather than attempting to derive legitimacy by linking present method to ancient authorities. Anti-pattern: attributing correctness to discoveries simply because they appear in ancients' works or forcing new particulars into older doctrines as exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize prematurely; pursue 'fitting certainty' via intermediate steps
rubrics_metrics.description: “We prohibit decisions and the laying down of certain principles, till we arrive regularly at generalities by the intermediate steps... Our object is not uncertainty but fitting certainty.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict generalization until proper inductive steps and intermediate propositions have been established by observation and experiment. Prefer knowing what is necessary over assuming full possession of truth. Anti-pattern: leaping to universal principles from insufficient instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the inductive method across all sciences, including moral and political
rubrics_metrics.description: “We certainly intend to comprehend them all... so our inductive method likewise comprehends them all. For we form a history and tables of invention for anger, fear, shame... as well as for heat and cold, light, vegetation, and the like.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct histories and tables of instances for mental operations and civil life as well as physical phenomena; adapt doctrine of interpretation to regulate the mind's application to the nature of subjects. Example: create histories for emotions and mental operations to derive principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and respect existing arts and sciences for their social and pedagogical roles
rubrics_metrics.description: “We readily cherish their practice, cultivation, and honor; for we by no means interfere to prevent the prevalent system from encouraging discussion, adorning discourses, or being employed serviceably in the chair of the professor or the practice of common life...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the new method is not designed to supplant all current practices immediately; existing methods serve teaching, rhetoric, and everyday use. Anti-pattern: claiming the new method should instantly replace all academic or popular modes of instruction and discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value invention as one of the highest ends of science
rubrics_metrics.description: “The introduction of great inventions appears one of the most distinguished of human actions... the benefits derived from inventions may extend to mankind in general... Inventions are also, as it were, new creations and imitations of divine works.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize work that extends human command over nature through arts and sciences; note examples of transformative inventions (printing, gunpowder, the compass) that changed the world. Consider ambition that enlarges human power over things as noble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on systematic rules and demonstrations rather than individual talent
rubrics_metrics.description: “Our method of discovering the sciences merely levels men's wits, and leaves but little to their superiority, since it achieves everything by the most certain rules and demonstrations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design methods so that reliable rules and demonstrations produce results independent of exceptional individual genius. Expect method to attribute success more to time/fortune and procedure than to isolated talent. Anti-pattern: overvaluing solitary brilliance when a rule-based method can be followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: The art of interpretation is useful but imperfect; two commitments are required
rubrics_metrics.description: “If men had at their command a proper history of nature and experience, and would apply themselves steadily to it, and could bind themselves to two things: 1, to lay aside received opinions and notions; 2, to restrain themselves, till the proper season, from generalization, they might... fall into our way of interpretation without the aid of any art.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When practicing interpretation, actively set aside received opinions and delay generalization until warranted. The art is a facilitation; with disciplined practice and the two commitments the interpretive method becomes natural and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute abstract demonstration for experimental verification
rubrics_metrics.description: “Forms of demonstration... are absolutely required to generalize the results of experience... so far as they rise above experience... they are essential; but... they become detrimental when obtruded in the place of direct experiment, or employed as a means of deducing conclusions about nature from imaginary hypotheses and abstract conceptions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deductive/formal demonstrations to organize and extend experimentally grounded results, not as a replacement for experiment. Anti-pattern: the Greek and scholastic tendency to remove principles from experimental test and deduce nature from abstract axioms alone.
